title: Before You Say Another Word
author: Antonius Veritas
summary: Antonius Veritas opens with Odysseus taunting the blinded Cyclops as he escapes, a moment of pride that hands his enemy the means to curse his homecoming. He uses the story to argue that most of us are Odysseus, speaking from pride, anger, anxiety or boredom rather than necessity. Drawing on Epictetus, Enchiridion 33, he recommends disciplining speech by talking only when necessary and with restraint. The core practice is to ask what is compelling you to speak and to question the impression that you need to say something. He then offers concrete exercises: notice your tendencies to advise, interrupt, exaggerate or one-up, let others finish, admit when you do not know, defer speech when angry and offer advice only when asked. Restraint, he concludes, builds the sense of timing that makes warnings, disagreement and humor land well.
points: Pride, anger, anxiety and boredom often drive speech, so the Stoic question to ask is what is compelling you to speak.
Epictetus advises speaking only when necessary and with restraint, and steering conversation away from gossip and comparison toward worthwhile matters.
Intelligence is often used to justify impulsiveness, so being clever offers no protection against saying something damaging.
Practice means noticing your habits, letting others finish, saying you do not know, deferring speech when angry and giving advice only when asked.
Restraint develops timing, which keeps warnings, disagreement and apologies from backfiring and preserves your influence.
quotes: He wants the creature to know who defeated him. So he etches his name, his father’s name and where he hails from in the blue sky.
It’s easy for a whiff of anger to animate words that break a relationship.
And looking back, intelligence is often useless when we use it justify impulsiveness.
This is why Epictetus in Enchiridion 33 advises us to discipline our speech. To speak only when necessary and with restraint.
This is why it’s necessary to ask yourself this question at any given moment- What is compelling me to speak?

Pride wants everyone to know you’re the shit. Anger insists kindness is weakness. Anxiety wants you to fill the silence with meaningless chatter. Boredom makes people’s private lives all the more entertaining.
You let the other person finish without interjecting. You say you don’t know when you don’t have enough information to form an opinion. You defer speaking when you’re angry.
And through restraint you master the art of timing. You don’t want to give necessary warnings, disagree or apologize at the wrong time.
